subject: Copywriting
title: New Coke: The Taste of a New Generation Gone Wrong
description: One-minute skill: New Coke: The Taste of a New Generation Gone Wrong.

hook.text: In 1985, Coca-Cola changed its formula and launched 'The Best Just Got Better.' 400,000 angry letters proved otherwise.

buildup.text: Pepsi's 'The Choice of a New Generation' had been winning blind taste tests. Coke panicked and reformulated.

discovery.text: The new slogan ignored what Coke actually was: nostalgia, tradition, Americana. No slogan could sell a betrayal.

twist.text: Coke brought back the original as 'Coca-Cola Classic' and sales soared.

climax.text: The lesson: a slogan can't fix a bad product decision. Copy serves the brand, not the other way around.

punchline.text: 400,000 angry letters. No slogan can sell a betrayal.

quiz.question: How many complaint letters did Coca-Cola receive about New Coke?

details.summary: In 1985, Coca-Cola reformulated its recipe and launched New Coke, positioning it against Pepsi's 'New Generation' messaging. The backlash was immediate and ferocious. Customers didn't want a new taste — they wanted the brand's heritage. Coca-Cola retreated to 'Classic Coke' within 79 days.
details.whyItMatters: New Coke shows that slogans and branding cannot override deep emotional connections to a product. When a slogan contradicts what customers love about a brand, disaster follows.
takeaways: Coca-Cola underestimated the emotional attachment to its original recipe
Taste tests favored New Coke, but emotional loyalty favored the original
The company recovered by rebranding the original as Coca-Cola Classic

faq.question: If New Coke tasted better in tests, why did it fail?
faq.answer: Blind taste tests measured flavor preference, not emotional connection. People drank Coca-Cola for nostalgia, comfort, and identity — not just taste. Changing the recipe felt like betraying a relationship, not just swapping a flavor.

faq.question: Was the New Coke failure actually a marketing success?
faq.answer: Some conspiracy theorists claim it was deliberate, but insiders confirm it was a genuine mistake. However, the outcry and triumphant return of Classic Coke did reinforce how much people loved the brand, generating massive free publicity.
